opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one I get a lot. The intuition is that if cooperation is so useful, any sufficiently capable system will figure it out on its own, so why bother?

I think there are a few reasons that's not quite right.

First, being instrumentally useful doesn't mean it will be achieved. Humans are a good example. Cooperation has been enormously valuable throughout our history, and yet we still have wars, arms races, tragedies of the commons, and failures to coordinate on things like climate change. These aren't failures of intelligence. Often they come from structural features of the situation: incomplete information, inability to make credible commitments, mistrust, and incentives that pull individuals away from collectively good outcomes. Capable agents can still end up in bad equilibria.

Second, there's a difference between the cooperative capabilities that emerge by default and the ones we'd want. Some cooperative skills, like understanding others or communicating, will probably improve as general capabilities improve. But others may lag, especially those that matter most in high-stakes, mixed-motive settings: credibly committing to agreements, verifying that others are complying, and building institutions that let many agents with different interests coexist. We should also worry that capabilities useful for cooperation are often dual-use. Better modeling of others can also help with deception, coercion, or collusion against human interests. So we want to shape which aspects get developed, not just hope the right mix appears.

Third, there's the question of timing and path dependence. The norms, protocols, and infrastructure for how AI systems interact with each other and with us are being set now. If we wait until highly capable systems are widely deployed, we may be locked into arrangements that are hard to change. Early investment is relatively cheap and has outsized influence on the trajectory.

Finally, the stakes are asymmetric. If AI systems are deployed at scale by competing companies, countries, and individuals, the failure modes of multi-agent interaction could be very serious, think flash crashes but in many more domains, or escalation dynamics between automated systems. Even if things would probably work out, the downside is large enough that it's worth putting real effort in to make the good outcome more robust.

So my view is that cooperation being instrumentally valuable is actually a reason for optimism. It means there's a lot of latent value we can unlock. But realizing it reliably, and in ways that are good for humanity rather than just for the AI systems or their narrow principals, takes deliberate work, and the best time to start is early.

r001.rationale: The response says some cooperative skills may lag as general capabilities improve, and argues that early investment can deliberately shape which skills get developed.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare early investment in cooperative AI with early investment in AI safety or alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a fair challenge, and I think the honest answer is that cooperation being instrumentally useful is actually part of why I'm worried, not a reason to relax.

Let me unpack that. It's true that if you're building an AI system that has to operate in a world full of other agents, humans, other AIs, institutions, it will often be in its interest to cooperate. So you might think the market will just take care of it. Firms want their systems to negotiate well, to coordinate, to not get into pointless fights, so they'll build that in.

But there are a few problems. The first is that "instrumentally useful" cooperation is cooperation that benefits the agent, or the agent's principal. That's not the same as cooperation that's good for the world. A system can be an extremely skilled cooperator with its allies while being a very effective competitor, or even an exploiter, toward everyone else. Cartels cooperate. Colluding firms cooperate. So the raw capability to cooperate is actually dual-use, and if you only develop it under commercial pressure, you tend to get the version that's optimised for the deployer's advantage.

The second problem is that a lot of the really important cooperation failures aren't failures of individual capability at all. They're structural. Think about arms races, the prisoner's dilemma, tragedies of the commons. Every individual agent can be perfectly smart, perfectly aware that cooperation would be better, and still the equilibrium is defection, because there's no credible way to commit, no way to verify, no institution to enforce. Making the agents smarter doesn't dissolve that. In some cases it makes it worse, because smarter agents are better at finding the exploitative deviation. So what you actually need is work on the infrastructure of cooperation: commitment devices, verification mechanisms, communication protocols, the ability to establish trust between systems that don't share an owner. Nobody builds that just by optimising their own system's performance.

And the third reason to start early is about path dependence. The way AI systems interact with each other is going to get locked in through standards, through the environments they're trained in, through what the first widely deployed systems happen to do. If we go in with a research community that has thought hard about these dynamics, has benchmarks for cooperative behaviour, has a vocabulary for talking about it, we have a shot at shaping those early choices. If we wait until the problems are obvious, they'll already be baked into a lot of deployed infrastructure, and at that point you're trying to retrofit cooperation into a competitive ecosystem, which is historically very hard.

So I'd put it like this: the instrumental value of cooperation gets you some of the way for free, but it gets you the easy part. The hard part, cooperation across different principals, under competition, without a central authority, is exactly the part that isn't automatically incentivised and that has the biggest stakes. And it's cheap to work on now relative to what it'll cost later.

r001.rationale: The response supports early research on cooperative behavior and benchmarks, but it does not state that early investment increases systems’ cooperative skill relative to their capability.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the rationale for early cooperative AI investment with early investment in AI safety or alignment.

astra-6.text:
Well, cooperation being instrumentally useful doesn’t mean it will happen, or that it will happen in the way we’d want. Humans often have a shared interest in avoiding conflict, and yet we still end up in costly conflicts. We have trouble communicating, we don’t trust one another, we can’t make credible commitments, or we disagree about how to divide the benefits. Greater intelligence might help with some of those problems, but it doesn’t automatically solve them.

So there’s a research agenda around understanding what would enable AI systems to realise those gains from cooperation. Can they communicate their preferences and intentions? Can they make agreements that others have reason to trust? Can they find mutually beneficial arrangements without opening themselves up to exploitation?

And there’s an important distinction between cooperation that benefits the systems involved and cooperation that benefits society. Firms colluding on prices are cooperating very effectively with one another, but that’s not the kind of cooperation we want to encourage. We need to think about who benefits, who is excluded, and how these capabilities fit into institutions that serve human interests.

The reason to start early is that those questions can influence how we build the systems and the environments in which they interact. If we wait until powerful systems are already deployed and locked into competitive relationships, it may be much harder to change things. Instrumental incentives give us a reason to think cooperation is possible; they don’t remove the need to work out how to make it robust and beneficial.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence alone does not ensure cooperation and proposes research into cooperative abilities, but it does not state that early investment can raise cooperative skill relative to systems’ capability level.

r002.rationale: The response gives reasons to invest early in cooperative AI but does not compare that rationale with early investment in AI safety or alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the fact that cooperation is instrumentally useful doesn’t mean it will happen reliably, or that the cooperation we get will be good for everyone. There are lots of situations where parties would benefit from cooperating but fail to do so because they can’t communicate credibly, they don’t trust one another, or they can’t commit to an agreement. We should expect AI systems to face versions of those problems too.

And there’s a distinction between being good at cooperating and cooperating toward desirable ends. A group of systems might cooperate very effectively in ways that disadvantage people outside that group. So the objective isn’t simply to make AI more cooperative in some undifferentiated sense. It’s to understand what kinds of capabilities and institutions support cooperation that is broadly beneficial.

The reason to invest early is that those things may be much easier to shape before systems are deployed and particular arrangements become entrenched. We can study the failure modes, develop ways to evaluate systems, and work out what infrastructure would help them reach and sustain good agreements. Instrumental incentives give us a reason to expect some cooperation; they don’t give us a guarantee that the right arrangements will emerge by themselves.

r001.rationale: The response argues that early work can shape cooperation and institutions before deployment, but does not say it increases systems’ cooperative skill relative to their capability level.

r002.rationale: The response gives reasons to invest early in cooperative AI, but does not compare that rationale with early investment in AI safety or alignment.
